title: Emor: say it twice (Leviticus 21:1)
hookLine: "speak" and "say" are doubled; Rashi reads it as elders teaching the young

lines: LOOK BOTH WAYS. SAY THANK YOU.
cards: Look both ways. Say thank you. Call your grandmother.

Some phrases get said in a family so often they wear a groove. A child groans at them. Then, years later, the same words come out of that child's mouth, to a kid of their own, or a niece, or a new hire at work.
The next portion of Leviticus is named Emor, say. And its first verse has a small oddity: God tells Moses to speak to the priests, and then, in the same breath, to say to them. Why both?

teach.b: The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Speak unto the priests the sons of Aaron, and say unto them". In Hebrew, emor, say, and then ve-amarta, and you shall say.
Two forms of the same verb, one right after the other.
A rabbinic principle: the Torah doesn't waste words. If something seems repeated, it's there to teach something more.

teach.h: RASHI: THE ADULTS, FOR THE YOUNG.
teach.b: Rashi, drawing on the Talmud, says the doubling is there to charge the adults regarding the young. The law that follows is about priests keeping away from contact with the dead, except for close family.
The grown priests are told: it isn't enough to keep this yourselves. You're responsible for your children keeping it too. One say for you, one say for them.
Later teachers take Rashi's reading further.

teach.h: SAID ONCE BY DOING, ONCE BY TEACHING.
teach.b: Every generation says it twice: once by doing it, and once by teaching it. A practice that isn't passed on lasts exactly one lifetime.
The Shema says it too: teach these words diligently to your children. And notice how Rashi phrases it: the adults are warned about the young.
The responsibility runs downhill, from the ones who know to the ones still learning. Whatever you've learned on this path, someone around you hasn't heard it yet.

how: Jewish tradition treats teaching the next generation as a commandment, from the Shema's command to teach these words to one's children, and the Passover seder is built around children's questions and adults' answers.

practice: Think of something you've picked up, on these four hundred days or anywhere else in your life: a word, a story, a habit, a skill.
Think of someone younger or newer who might like to know it, a child, a niece, a colleague just starting out, and imagine how you'd say it in a sentence or two.
